summary: Count: to 100 by ones and tens, and backward from 30.
Count backward from 30 by ones.
Write the numbers 0 to 20.
Write a numeral 0 to 20 to show how many objects, with 0 meaning none.
Given a number from 1 to 20, count out that many objects.
Count to answer "how many?" for up to 20 objects in a line, array or circle.
Count to answer "how many?" for up to 10 scattered objects.
Break numbers up to 10 into parts, and show equality as a balance.
Break numbers into two groups in more than one way and record each with a drawing or equation.
Use objects or drawings to show that an equation balances equal amounts.
Sort objects or people into categories by attribute, with up to 10 in each.
Recognize and name pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters.
Describe things around you using shape names.
Describe where things are using words like above, below, in front of, behind and next to.
Add and subtract within 10 fluently.
Add and subtract within 20 using strategies like counting on, making 10 and known facts.
Count forward and back to 120 and read, write and show numbers in that range.
Count forward to 120 and backward from 120, starting at any number below 120.
Read and write numerals to 120 and use them to show how many objects.
Add within 100 using models, drawings, place value, properties, or the add-subtract relationship.
Record the addition strategy in writing, explain it, and know tens add to tens and ones to ones.
Subtract multiples of 10 using models, drawings, place value, properties, or the add-subtract relationship.
Record the subtraction strategy in writing and explain the reasoning.
Tell time to the hour and half hour, and know the values of coins.
Know the value of a penny, nickel, dime and quarter.
Investigate questions with categorical data: pose a question, gather, organize and interpret data.
Pose a question that can be answered by collecting data.
Decide how to collect data from classmates.
Organize and show data in a table or chart with up to three categories.
Answer questions about the table or chart: totals, each category, and how many more or fewer.
Put flat shapes together to make new and composite shapes.
Put solid shapes together to make a composite shape, then new shapes from it.
Add and subtract within 20 fluently using mental strategies; knowing facts from memory is not stated.
Count forward and backward within 1,000; skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s.
Add and subtract within 1,000 with models, drawings or strategies, and connect them to equations.
Solve add and subtract money word problems within 100, using $ or ¢ but not both, no decimals.
Investigate a measurement question: collect length data and show it on a dot plot.
Identify a statistical question about measurements.
Measure several objects, or one object repeatedly, to the nearest whole unit.
Show measurement data on a dot plot with a whole-number scale.
Fluently multiply and divide within 100 using strategies; knowing all products from memory is not stated.
Tell time to the minute and solve elapsed-time problems within and across the hour.
Measure and solve problems with mass and liquid volume.
Measure and estimate mass and liquid volume in grams, kilograms and liters.
Solve one-step word problems about masses or volumes in the same units, with any operation.
Investigate questions with categorical data using scaled picture and bar graphs.
Identify a statistical question about categorical data and collect the data.
Make a scaled picture graph and scaled bar graph of a data set, by hand or with technology.
Answer how-many-more and how-many-fewer questions from the graph about the question posed.
Investigate questions with numerical data using measurements and dot plots.
Identify a statistical question about numerical data.
Measure lengths with rulers marked in halves and fourths of an inch.
Show the data on a dot plot marked in whole numbers, halves or quarters.
Describe the shape of the data on the plot and compare answers to the question posed.
Solve real-world and math problems about perimeters of polygons.
Find a polygon's perimeter from its side lengths.
Find a missing side length from the perimeter and the other sides.
Draw rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas, or the same area but different perimeters.
Classify polygons by sides and vertices, and quadrilaterals by their attributes.
Sort polygons by number of sides and vertices: triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons.
Classify rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses and trapezoids, seeing shared attributes define larger groups.
Identify shapes that do not belong to a given category or subcategory.
Solve multistep problems, including using the conventional order of operations.
Do operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses.
Find factors and multiples of numbers from 1 to 100.
Find all factor pairs of a whole number up to 100.
Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors.
Tell whether a whole number up to 100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number.
Tell whether a whole number up to 100 is prime or composite.
Read, write and compare multi-digit whole numbers.
Read and write multi-digit whole numbers in numerals, words and expanded form.
Compare multi-digit whole numbers by place value using >, = and <.
Understand and make equivalent fractions.
Use visual models to find equivalent fractions with different numerators and denominators.
Explain why multiplying top and bottom by the same number gives an equivalent fraction.
Convert and add fractions with denominators 10 and 100.
Rewrite a fraction in tenths as an equivalent fraction in hundredths.
Add a fraction in tenths to a fraction in hundredths.
Compare two decimals to hundredths.
Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size.
Know decimal comparisons only make sense when both refer to the same whole.
Record decimal comparisons with >, = or < and justify them.
Understand how units relate within a measurement system.
Within one system, express a measurement in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit.
Record measurement equivalents in a two-column table.
Solve measurement problems with whole numbers, simple fractions or decimals.
Solve problems that convert a measurement from a larger unit to a smaller one in the same system.
Show measurement quantities on diagrams with a scale, such as number lines.
Use dot plots of fractional measurements to answer a statistical question.
Identify a statistical question about numerical data.
Make a dot plot of measurements in halves, quarters and eighths of a unit.
Add and subtract fractions to solve problems using a dot plot.
Recognize a line of symmetry in a flat figure.
Identify line-symmetric figures and draw their lines of symmetry.
Make number patterns for situations and show the relationship in tables, ordered pairs and graphs.
Find the rule for a growing pattern, relating corresponding terms (x, y).
Make patterns from one or two given rules (x, y).
Show the relationship between pattern quantities with tables, ordered pairs and graphs.
Fluently multiply whole numbers, up to four digits by two digits, using an algorithm.
Divide up to four-digit numbers by two-digit numbers using place value, properties or multiplication.
Show and explain the division with equations, arrays or area models.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals to hundredths with models, drawings or strategies.
Record the decimal strategy in writing and explain the reasoning.
Add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with unlike denominators by reasoning or common denominators.
Solve word problems adding and subtracting fractions of the same whole, including unlike denominators.
Use benchmark fractions to estimate and check whether fraction answers make sense.
Gather categorical and numerical data for statistical questions, choose a bar graph, pictograph or dot plot, and interpret.

state_code: # SOURCES (Kentucky Academic Standards for Mathematics, adopted 2019, document v1.4 7/1/19)
# - No official KAS-vs-CCSS crosswalk was found; rows were compared to CCSS text directly. KY moves most examples into a "Clarifications" column (not read as standard text).
# - KY lists lettered sub-parts under many standards and refers to them as codes (e.g. KY.1.MD.3b, KY.3.NF.3d in coherence notes), so each gets a row.
# CCSS K-5 STANDARDS DROPPED: none entirely. Partly changed:
# - Line plots become dot plots, with "statistical question" sub-parts added (an idea CCSS starts in 6.SP.A.1): KY.2.MD.9, KY.3.MD.3, KY.3.MD.4, KY.4.MD.4, KY.5.MD.2.
# - K.MD.B.3: counting categories and sorting them by count is not in the KY text.
# - 2.OA.B.2 / 3.OA.C.7: "know from memory" is not in the standard text (may be in clarifications).
# - 5.MD.B.2: fraction line plot replaced by choosing a display for categorical/numerical data.
# - 3.G.A.1: now also classifies polygons by sides (from 2.G.A.1) and lists parallelograms and trapezoids.
# - KDE began reviewing the KAS for Mathematics in fall 2025 (advisory panel/review committee meetings through spring and June 2026). I found no adopted replacement,
#   so the 2019 standards are assumed in effect for 2026-27; check for a new version before relying on this for 2027-28.
# - KY.K.CC.1b (count back from 30) and KY.K.OA.3b (equality as balance) are marked "new"; KY.K.MD.4 and KY.1.MD.3b (coins) "moved" from 2.MD.C.8;
#   KY.4.OA.3a (order of operations without parentheses) "moved" from the 3.OA.D.8 footnote. Judgement calls.
# - Text was extracted from a two-column PDF table; equation images lose fraction symbols, which does not affect the codes or mappings.
# - CCSS baseline: CCSS Math PDF, https://corestandards.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/Math_Standards1.pdf ; ccss codes are expanded with cluster letters from the CCSS K-5 list.
# - kind is judged on content, not code: a state standard that only renames/recodes or drops/moves examples into notes is "same".
# - Lettered sub-parts get their own row (with a stem row when the stem has its own text). A sub-part that mirrors a CCSS sub-part is "same";
#   a sub-part carved out of a CCSS standard that has no such sub-part (e.g. a split of one CCSS sentence into a/b) is "edited" with a summary.
# - Sub-part rows list the parent CCSS code (CCSS sub-part letters are not used in the ccss column).
# - "moved" is used when the main content comes from another CCSS grade; the other grade's code is in ccss.
